OR compartmentalization5,15, verified by in situ Hi-C (Extended Data 
Fig. 3e–g). Finally, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of the cultured GFP+ 
OSNs and direct comparison with primary GFP+ OSNs shows equally 
strong Olfr17 transcription and minimal detection of other OR mRNAs 
(Extended Data Fig. 3h).
To image LHX2 and EBF1 proteins, we knocked in HaloTag37 to the 
endogenous Lhx2 and Ebf1 alleles, generating C-terminal HaloTag 
fusions (schematics in Fig. 3a,b) expressed at endogenous levels. 
Homozygote Lhx2-HaloTag mice are viable with fully developed 
MOEs, whereas homozygote Ebf1-HaloTag mice have normal numbers 
of B cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Thus, HaloTags do not disrupt LHX2 
and EBF1 function, which would lead to embryonic lethality38 and 
deficient B cell differentiation39, respectively. We crossed these mice 
with Gng8-tTA/tetO-Olfr17-ires-GFP mice, and cultured primary OSNs. 
Of note, we detected numerous Halo-labelled foci of local LHX2 or 
EBF1 accumulation (Fig. 3c,d). Focal TF distribution is consistent with 
the observation that every OSN contains around six major GIHs and 
tens of pairs or triplets of interacting GIs, especially at less differenti-
ated OSNs. Beyond GIHs, these foci might represent multi-enhancer 
hubs assembled by non-GI CREs that contain composite motifs. Con-
sistent with this, if we calculate the median strength of GI–GI trans 
contacts in Olfr17-expressing OSNs, we identify hundreds of trans 
interactions between LHX2-bound, composite-containing CREs in 
the OSN genome that reach this threshold (Fig. 3e,f). Thus, com-
posite sequences might drive the assembly of many multi-enhancer 
hubs in OSNs, explaining the high number of LHX2 and EBF1 foci. 
Gene ontology (GO) analysis of genes near interchromosomal hubs 
defined by a stringent cut-off (normalized contact probability > 3) 
suggests a connection with cellular differentiation and neuronal 
morphogenesis (Fig. 3i).
Solid condensates form in OSNs
To decipher LHX2 and EBF1 dynamics, we performed single-molecule 
tracking in cultured OSNs. We compared the mobility of LHX2 and EBF1, 
in their respective foci, to the mobility of these protein molecules when 
they are free in the nucleoplasm (that is, unincorporated into foci). We 
also infected OSNs with HaloTag-NLS (a nuclear localization signal), 
to measure nuclear HaloTag mobility in the absence of restrictive 
nucleoprotein interactions. We tracked molecules at around 49.99 Hz 
and plotted displacements between frames (Fig. 4a–f). We observed 
that most HaloTag–LHX2 and HaloTag–EBF1 displacements fall within 
our localization error (around 20 nm; details in Methods), whereas the 
HaloTag-NLS displacements are much longer, consistent with free diffu-
sion. To ascertain the fraction bound and the diffusion coefficient of the 
unbound fraction, we performed a two-state modelling of the measured 
displacements using Spot-On, a modelling framework that accounts 
for known biases in single-molecule tracking, such as faster-moving 
molecules moving out of focus40. We found that 92% of LHX2 is in a 
bound state and 76% of EBF1 is in a bound state. We then looked at indi-
vidual trajectories and categorized each localization within a trajec-
tory as inside or outside a condensate, on the basis of local density of 
localizations at a 20-nm radius (Fig. 4g). Subsequently, we plotted the 
average mean squared displacement for trajectories that were either 
entirely outside or entirely inside condensates (Fig. 4h). We observed 
that the free LHX2 and EBF1 molecules were displaced by an average 
of 330 nm (LHX2) and 430 nm (EBF1) within 80 ms—approaching the 
mobility of HaloTag-NLS (530 nm within 80 ms). In the same timeframe, 
incorporated LHX2 and EBF1 molecules cover less than 100 nm, with 
little exchange between incorporated and free molecules (Fig. 4g). 
Consistent with this, in vivo FRAP showed little fluorescent recovery 
of the photobleached foci even after 10 min (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). 
Treating OSNs with 1.5% 1,6-hexanediol for 30 min did not cause dis-
solution of LHX2- or EBF1-containing condensates. In these conditions, 
HaloTag–BRD4-containing condensates with liquid phase properties41 
are significantly diminished, owing to 1,6-hexanediol-induced dis-
solution (Extended Data Fig. 4c–e). Therefore, LHX2 and EBF1 form 
stable condensates in vivo, confirming the solid properties of the 
in-vitro-assembled GIHs.
To track the dynamics of LHX2 and EBF1 proteins over longer time-
frames, we performed a pulse-chase experiment that differentially 
labelled ‘old’ and ‘new’ proteins. We first provide a ‘red’ Halo ligand 
at saturating concentrations, labelling all the existing LHX2 or EBF1 
proteins for 24 h. Then, we wash away the unincorporated ligand, 
and add a second ‘far-red’ Halo ligand, at a window of 24 h (or 72 h), 
labelling only newly translated proteins (Fig. 4i). We first applied this 
protocol to the study of HaloTag–BRD4 condensates, which revealed 
that around 90% of the condensates contain both new (far-red) and 
old (red) BRD4 proteins (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 5a), consistent 
with liquid properties. By contrast, LHX2 and EBF1 condensates pre-
dominantly contain proteins of the same age (that is, only red or far-red 
proteins per condensate), with only 39% and 46% of the condensates 
containing both new and old LHX2 and EBF1, respectively (Fig. 4k,l and 
Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Thus, live imaging on sub-second, minute 
and multi-day scales confirms that LHX2 and EBF1 have the propensity 
to form complexes with unusually high protein stability and minimal 
protein exchange.
Solid condensates engage active ORs
We next asked whether the LHX2 and EBF1-containing condensates 
represent transcriptionally engaged hubs. We devised a strategy 
for fluorescent labelling of the transcriptionally active Olfr17 allele 
in cultured OSNs, because this allele is attached to one of the LHX2–
EBF1–LDB1-containing multi-enhancer hubs. We used single guide 
RNAs (sgRNAs) to direct dCas9 to the GFP-tagged Olfr17 allele, and 
incorporated a signal amplification system (SunTag-scFV-mKate242) 
that would enable visualization of the unique Olfr17 locus (Fig. 5a). We 
delivered seven sgRNAs, dCAS9-SunTag and scFV-mKate2 with three 
different lentiviruses that co-infected the cultured GFP+ OSNs, suc-
cessfully labelling and visualizing the transcriptionally active OR allele 
(Fig. 5b). Consistent with the hypothesis that solid phase transitions 
drive the assembly of transcriptionally competent GIHs, we observe 
overlap between Olfr17 and LHX2–EBF1 condensates in most OSN 
nuclei (Fig. 5c,d and Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7). On average, LHX2 and 
EBF1 condensates reside within 245 nm and within 214 nm from Olfr17 
(Fig. 5i), respectively, a spatial proximity consistent with transcription-
ally relevant engagement43. We could not perform single-molecule 
tracking or FRAP exclusively at these condensates, because of rapid 
photobleaching of the fluorescent signal on Olfr17. Owing to a lack 
of available colours, we could not perform pulse-chase experiments 
with two fluorescent Halo ligands either. Instead, we labelled LHX2 
and EBF1 for 24 h with a far-red ligand that was washed and replaced 
with saturating concentrations of a ‘dark’ ligand, ensuring that only 
proteins expressed during the 24-h window are fluorescent. We imaged 
OSNs 24 h and 48 h after washing the far-red ligand, and identified 
numerous OSNs with old LHX2- and EBF1-containing condensates 
within 250 nm from the active Olfr17 allele (Fig. 5e–i and Extended Data 
Figs. 8–10). Thus, solid-like LHX2–EBF1 condensates are compatible 
with OR transcription.
Discussion
Our data suggest that the underlying DNA sequence influences 
the homotypic properties of LHX2–EBF1–LDB1 bound across the 
genome, instructing highly specific and unusually stable contacts 
between similar complexes over vast genomic distances. GIH assem-
bly might be the consequence of DNA-sequence-induced structural 
reorganization of LHX2–EBF1–LDB1; reorganization caused by the 
unique arrangement of the three proteins on the composite motif; 

Nature  |  Vol 643  |  17 July 2025  |  825
or both. Resistance to 1,6-hexanediol dissolution suggests that the 
proposed DNA-sequence-induced allostery does not expose IDRs with 
weak, self-interacting properties44,45, but rather, structured surfaces 
with a high affinity and specificity for similarly exposed surfaces 
from LHX2–EBF1–LDB1 complexes on other GIs. The identification 
of LHX2–LHX9–LEF1-motif-containing range-extending elements 
(REXs) that promote long-range genomic interactions in the mouse 
limb46, together with the finding that LDB1 regulates widespread 
assembly of multi-enhancer hubs in erythroblasts47, suggest that 
this presumed version of DNA-induced allostery is not exclusive to

Article
GIs and OSNs. However, the high concentration of optimal compos-
ite motifs in GIs might distinguish them from other CREs, creating 
a three-tier system in genome organization: GIs with the ability to 
interact with each other across chromosomes; long-range CREs and 
REXs that make contacts over long distances within chromosomes; 
and local CREs that are also bound by LHX2–EBF1–LDB1 but lack the 
sequence features for long-range action. OR promoters, which con-
tain LHX2 and EBF1 motifs but lack composite motifs22,23, would be 
assigned to the third tier, which explains why their recruitment to 
GIHs requires continuous transcription; if the nascent OR mRNA 
facilitates recruitment to GIHs18, OR transcription would compensate 
for the considerable depletion of composite motifs from OR promot-
ers. Thus, although many GIHs can stably form in an OSN nucleus, 
transcription-dependent OR recruitment and an RNA-mediated 
symmetry-breaking process18 ensure that only one OR allele is stably 
transcribed in each OSN.
Our discovery raises questions about the value of solid instead 
of liquid phase transitions in genome architecture. Liquid phase 
separation provides an appealing explanation for the partition of 
the genome into megabase-scale compartments48, for the func-
tion of super-enhancers41, for heterochromatin spreading30,49 and 
for the assembly of the nucleolus50. In each case, large genomic 
segments converge in the nuclear space, exponentially enhanc-
ing weak, multivalent interactions through substantial increases 
in the concentrations of recurrent binders. In the case of GIHs or 
meta-domains1, however, the interacting DNA fragments are short 
(around 500 bp) and the total number of converging TF-binding 
sites is small, excluding a sharp increase in concentration as the 
cause of phase separation. Furthermore, weak affinities enhanced 
by liquid phase transitions, would ‘trap’ GIs locally, in contacts with 
numerous proximal DNA sequences bound by the same proteins. 
Thus, sequence-induced allostery followed by solid phase transitions 
might explain why certain DNA sequences ‘ignore’ proximal genomic 
partners with similar molecular (but not structural) valence and, 
instead, assemble specific and stable contacts over vast distances. 
The unusual stability that solid phase transitions confer to these 
interactions might represent a genome architecture ‘engram’ in 
the nucleus of post-mitotic cells. This engram explains the coun-
terintuitive observation that OR- and OSN-specific genes regulated 
by LHX2–EBF1–LDB1 are upregulated in mouse OSNs, whereas the 
expression of these proteins is downregulated18,19; if slow protein 
turnover preserves the structural and functional integrity of LHX2–
EBF1–LDB1 nucleoprotein condensates, then minimal synthesis of 
new proteins would suffice for stable and robust gene expression 
over the life of the OSN. This form of epigenetic memory could 
be deployed by every post-mitotic neuron that uses LHX2–LDB1 
complexes for its differentiation, because downregulating master 
regulators without altering nuclear architecture and transcriptional 
outputs could be crucial for the long-term maintenance of molecular 
and cellular identity.

===== Okashita2025_Nature_IronDeficiency-SexReversal =====

262  |  Nature  |  Vol 643  |  3 July 2025
Article
Maternal iron deficiency causes male-to- 
female sex reversal in mouse embryos
Naoki Okashita1, Ryo Maeda1, Shunsuke Kuroki1, Kyona Sasaki1, Yoko Uno1, Peter Koopman2 & 
Makoto Tachibana1 ✉
Ferrous iron (Fe2+) is essential in all eukaryotic cells for various oxidoreductase 
reactions, including the demethylation of DNA and proteins. Histone demethylation 
is required for normal epigenetic regulation of the Y-chromosomal sex-determining 
gene Sry in developing gonads during male sex determination1,2. Here we investigate 
the potential connection between iron metabolism, histone demethylation  
and sex determination in mammals. We found that Fe2+-producing pathways are 
substantially activated in mouse embryonic gonads during the sex-determining 
period. Chelation of iron in cultured XY gonads reduced the level of KDM3A-
mediated H3K9 demethylation of Sry, mostly abolished Sry expression and  
caused the gonads to express ovarian markers. In vivo, conditional deletion  
of the gene Tfrc—which is required for iron incorporation—in fetal XY gonadal 
somatic cells, or acute pharmaceutical suppression of available iron in pregnant 
mice, resulted in male-to-female gonadal sex reversal in a proportion of offspring, 
highlighting the pivotal role of iron metabolism in male sex determination. Finally, 
long-term feeding of pregnant mice with a low-iron diet, when combined with a 
heterozygous variant of Kdm3a that by itself has no observable effect, suppressed 
Sry expression and caused male-to-female sex reversal in some of the progeny, 
revealing a connection between maternal dietary iron and fetal developmental 
outcomes.
During sex determination in mammals, sexually bipotential gonads 
differentiate into testes as a result of expression of the testis- 
determining gene Sry (refs. 3,4). In mice, Sry expression is tightly 
regulated5; it is activated only in a subpopulation of gonadal somatic 
cells, termed pre-Sertoli cells, and only from embryonic day (E) 
10.5 to E12.5. The methylation of DNA and/or histones in chromatin 
influences the transcription of developmental genes, and we have 
previously shown that the JmjC-family H3K9 demethylase KDM3A, 
which is expressed predominantly in pre-Sertoli cells in deve­
loping gonads6, activates Sry by demethylating H3K9me2—a hall­
mark for transcriptionally suppressed heterochromatin—on the Sry 
locus1.
Iron has an indispensable role not only in the transport of oxy­
gen but also in a wide series of intracellular enzymatic reactions for 
oxidation and reduction. The JmjC-family histone demethylases 
require labile Fe2+ for their enzymatic activity. Iron metabolism 
is tightly regulated by cellular incorporation, utilization, stor-
age and excretion mechanisms7; however, the extent and nature 
of the cross-talk between iron metabolism and histone demeth-
ylation in development and physiology is largely unknown. Here 
we show that iron metabolism has a crucial function in KDM3A- 
mediated male sex determination in mice, revealing an unex-
pected link between metabolism and male sex determination in 
mammals.
 
Fe2+ actively accumulates in pre-Sertoli cells
The genes and proteins involved in cellular iron metabolism can be clas-
sified into three categories according to their functions: iron incorpora-
tion (Tfrc (encoding TFR1) and Scara5 (SCARA5)); Fe2+ production (Steap3 
(STEAP3), Slc11a2 (DMT1), Ncoa4 (NCOA4) and Hmox1 (HO1)); and 
iron excretion (Slc40a1 (FPN) and Heph (HEPH)) (Fig. 1a). We first exam­
ined the activity of these genes during mouse gonadal development.
We separated NR5A1+ gonadal somatic cells and NR5A1− mesonephric 
and germ cells from the gonads and mesonephros at the sex-determining 
period, E11.5, according to previously published methods1 (Extended 
Data Fig. 1a): only the former population contributes to sex determina-
tion. Quantitative mRNA expression analysis confirmed that the NR5A1+ 
fraction included Sry-expressing (pre-Sertoli) cells but the NR5A1− frac-
tion did not (Fig. 1b). Consistent with previous studies1,6, Kdm3a was 
expressed more abundantly in NR5A1+ than in NR5A1− cells (Fig. 1b). The 
iron-incorporation genes Tfrc and Scara5, and Fe2+-production genes 
Slc11a2, Steap3, Ncoa4 and Hmox1, were more abundant in NR5A1+ than 
in NR5A1− cells, but the reverse was true for the iron-excretion genes 
Slc40a1 and Heph (Fig. 1b). The mitochondrial Fe2+-incorporation gene 
Slc25A37 was less abundant in NR5A1+ than in NR5A1− cells (Extended 
Data Fig. 1b). Collectively, our gene-expression analysis indicates that 
Fe2+ accumulates in the cytosol and nucleus of the cells responsible for 
gonadal sex determination.

A previous study used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) 
analysis to study gene expression in different gonadal cellular com-
partments during mouse gonadal sex determination8. We analysed 
the resulting scRNA-seq dataset (available at the Gene Expression 
Omnibus (GEO) under GSE184708) to examine the expression pro-
files of the iron-metabolism-related genes in each cell type in E11.5 
gonads and mesonephros (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Consistent with 
our experimental findings above, mRNAs for iron-incorporation 
and Fe2+-production genes, as well as Kdm3a, were more abundantly 
expressed in pre-Sertoli cells than in the other gonadal cell types. We 
analysed scRNA-seq data of human XY developing gonads9, reveal-
ing that KDM3A and iron-incorporation, and Fe2+-production genes 
are expressed more abundantly in the cells responsible for male sex 
determination than in other cell types around the sex-determining 
period (Extended Data Fig. 1d).
We next examined the expression of iron-metabolic proteins in intact 
E11.5 XY gonads by immunofluorescence. NR5A1 and GATA4 proteins 
were used as markers for gonadal somatic cells. Iron-incorporating 
TFR1 and SCARA5, and Fe2+-producing NCOA4 and HO1, were more 
strongly detected in gonads than in other tissues, except for the liver, 
a major organ for iron storage (Fig. 1c). KDM3A was also highly 
expressed in gonads, consistent with previous findings1. We also 
examined the tissue distribution of these proteins by immunoblot-
ting (Fig. 1d). Iron-incorporating and Fe2+-producing proteins were 
found to be abundantly expressed in NR5A1+ gonadal cells, placenta 
and liver among E11.5 XY embryonic tissues and organs (Fig. 1d). To 
detect cellular labile Fe2+, we used the fluorescent probe FeRhoNox-1 
(ref. 10). As shown in Fig. 1e, fluorescence corresponding to Fe2+ was 
detected at high levels in E11.5 gonads.
Together, these data indicate a gene and protein expression profile 
that favours Fe2+ accumulation specifically in the gonadal cells that 
are responsible for sex determination. Accordingly, inductively cou-
pled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis showed that NR5A1+ 
cells contain 1.8 times more total iron (non-haem and haem) than do 
NR5A1− cells (Fig. 1f).

Fig. 1 | Iron-metabolism pathways are uniquely activated in embryonic 
gonads during male sex determination. a, Schematic representation of 
intracellular iron metabolism. TFR1 (encoded by Tfrc) and SCARA5 (Scara5) 
mediate iron incorporation through transferrin and ferritin, respectively. 
STEAP3 (Steap3) converts TFR1-dependently incorporated iron from Fe3+  
to Fe2+. DMT1 (Slc11a2) is a transporter of divalent metal ions including Fe2+.  
HO1 (Hmox1) produces Fe2+ by haem catabolism. NCOA4 (Ncoa4) upregulates 
cellular iron through ferritin degradation. FPN (Slc40a1) excretes Fe2+ from the 
cell, and HEPH (Heph) converts it to Fe3+. Red and blue text represents factors 
that increase and decrease intracellular Fe2+, respectively. b, Gene-expression 
analysis in NR5A1+ and NR5A1− cells using qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–
qPCR). Left, expression of Sry and Kdm3a. Right, expression of Tfrc and Scara5 
(iron incorporation), Steap3, Slc11a2, Ncoa4 and Hmox1 (Fe2+ production) and 
Slc40a1 and Heph (iron excretion). Numbers of embryos examined are shown at 
the top. Data are mean ± s.d. All differences between means with P < 0.01 are 
indicated; two-tailed paired t-tests. c, Immunofluorescence analysis for TFR1, 
SCARA5, NCOA4, HO1 and KDM3A in E11.5 XY embryos. Transverse sections with 
gonads and liver were used (bottom left). Gonads were counterstained with 
anti-GATA4 and anti-NR5A1 antibodies. White dashed lines outline gonads.  
Ao, aorta; Go, gonad; Li, liver; St, stomach. Scale bars, 5 μm (second from top); 
10 μm (all others). d, Comparison of the expression of iron-metabolism proteins 
and KDM3A among E11.5 embryonic tissues by immunoblotting. Relative values 
were calculated based on the signal of GAPDH. e, Fe2+-distribution analysis on 
the sections of E11.5 XY embryos, using a turn-on fluorescent probe (FeRhoNox-1) 
to detect labile Fe2+. White dashed lines outline gonads. Scale bar, 10 μm.  
f, Quantification of cellular iron in E11.5 NR5A1+ and NR5A− cells using ICP-MS. 
Numbers of experiments are shown at the top. Data are mean ± s.d. Differences 
between means with P < 0.01 are indicated; two-tailed paired t-tests.

genes. We focused on Tfrc (TFR1), which has a pivotal role in cellular iron 
incorporation through internalizing the transferrin–iron complex11. 
Because global null mutation of Tfrc leads to embryonic lethality before 
sex determination12, we used a strategy of disrupting Tfrc selectively in 
gonadal somatic cells before sex determination (Fig. 2a).
We inserted loxP sequences surrounding exon 3 of Tfrc to establish a 
conditional mutant allele of Tfrc (Tfrc2l) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We 
mated these mice with Wt1creERT2 mice, which can be induced by injec-
tion of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) to translocate Cre recombinase 
into the somatic cell nuclei of early-stage gonads. We injected 4-OHT 
into mothers carrying Wt1creERT2;Tfrc1l/2l mice at E8.5, and confirmed that 
TFR1 was specifically deleted in gonadal somatic cells in these embryos 
at E10.8 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 2c). Hereafter, we designate 
Wt1creERT2;Tfrc1l/2l embryos and mice that were administered 4-OHT at 
E8.5 as Tfrc1l/2l conditional knockout (Tfrc1l/2l-cKO) embryos and mice.
Labile Fe2+ was maintained at high levels in E10.8 XY control gonads 
(Fig. 2c), but was markedly decreased in XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO gonads 
(Fig. 2c), indicating that TFR1 depletion abrogates Fe2+ production 
before sex determination. We found that the number of NR5A1+ 
gonadal somatic cells in XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO gonads was comparable with 
that of control gonads at E11.5 (Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating 
that TFR1 depletion might not affect the growth potential of gonadal 
somatic cells. Total iron levels in XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO NR5A1+ cells were 
reduced to around half that in XY control NR5A1+ cells at E11.5 (Fig. 2d), 
and iron-storing H-ferritin in Tfrc1l/2l-cKO NR5A1+ cells were reduced 
to around one-third in XY NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

of Sry. a, Experimental scheme for establishing mice for gonadal-somatic-cell-

Nature  |  Vol 643  |  3 July 2025  |  265
Gonadal levels of H3K9me2 were considerably increased in E11.5 
XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO embryos (Fig. 2e). Quantification analysis showed 
that the levels of H3K9me2 in E11.5 XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO NR5A1+ cells were 
almost double those in control NR5A1+ cells (Fig. 2f). These findings 
suggested that H3K9 demethylation was compromised in gonadal 
somatic cells by TFR1 depletion. Quantitative mRNA expression analy-
sis indicated that levels of Sry mRNA expression were reduced in XY 
Tfrc1l/2l-cKO NR5A1+ cells to around half that in XY control NR5A1+ cells 
at E11.5 (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Notably, Hmox1, a gene for another 
Fe2+-production pathway (Fig. 1a), was upregulated in XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO 
NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 2e), suggesting a possible feedback 
mechanism compensating for Fe2+ deficiency.
Immunofluorescence analysis showed that averaged SRY expres-
sion in XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO gonads was around 50% of that in XY control 
gonads at E11.5 (Fig. 2g). To evaluate how TFR1 depletion influences 
H3K9me2 specifically at the Sry promoter, we performed chromatin 
immunoprecipitation followed by quantitative PCR (ChIP–qPCR) on 
isolated NR5A1+ cells (Fig. 2h). H3K9me2 levels at the Sry promoter in 
E11.5 XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO NR5A1+ cells were nearly twofold higher than those 
control NR5A1+ cells (Fig. 2h), suggesting a failure of H3K9 demethyla-
tion of the Sry locus.
We next examined internal and external genitalia in Tfrc1l/2l-cKO mice 
at the adolescent or adult stage. Notably, of 39 XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO mice, 
6 exhibited male-to-female sex reversal, with two ovaries, and one 
mouse was partially feminized with an ovary and a testis (Fig. 2i). By 
contrast, all XX Tfrc1l/2l-cKO adolescent mice seemed to develop into 
normal females (Extended Data Fig. 2f). The sex reversal phenotype 
of XY Tfrc1l/2l-cKO mice was similar to that of Kdm3a-deficient mice1. 
Together, our results indicate that correct iron balance in embryonic 
gonadal somatic cells is required for normal male sex determination 
in vivo, and implicate the TFR1-mediated iron-incorporating pathway 
in KDM3A-mediated epigenetic regulation of Sry.
Low iron levels impair Sry activation in gonads in vitro
To further clarify the mechanism by which iron deficiency influences 
gonadal sex determination, we developed an in vitro gonad culture 
system in which iron levels could be readily manipulated (Fig. 3a). In 
brief, segments of aorta, gonads, mesonephros and mesenchyme were 
isolated from E10.8 embryos, and then cultured on a membrane with 
different culture media.
Using standard culture medium, Sry expression in XY samples peaked 
after 19.2 h of culture, with expression levels comparable to those in 
E11.5 gonads in utero (Extended Data Fig. 3a). In XY or XX samples, 
culturing for a further 24 h (total 43.2 h) gave rise to sexually differ-
entiated gonads with either SOX9+ male-type somatic cells or FOXL2+ 
female-type somatic cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We refer to the initial 
19.2-h culture period and the subsequent 24-h period as pre- and post- 
differentiation, respectively.
We added an iron-specific chelator, deferoxamine (DFO)13 into the 
medium during pre-differentiation (Fig. 3a). We found that the number 
of NR5A1+ cells was indistinguishable between DFO-treated gonads 
and untreated gonads (Extended Data Fig. 3b), indicating that DFO 
treatment did not affect the growth potential of gonadal somatic cells. 
Direct iron measurement by ICP-MS revealed that cellular iron levels in 
NR5A1+ cells were reduced to about 40% by DFO treatment (Fig. 3b). We 
also found that treatment with DFO caused a marked reduction in the 
levels of iron-storing H-ferritin and L-ferritin in NR5A1+ cells, to around 
one-fifth that in untreated NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c). These 
data confirmed that cellular iron levels were substantially reduced by 
DFO treatment.
We evaluated gonadal sex differentiation in the treated cultures by 
calculating the number of FOXL2+ and SOX9+ cells. The proportion 
of FOXL2+ cells in untreated XY gonads was 0%, but reached nearly 
90% in DFO-treated XY gonads (Fig. 3c). DFO treatment did not affect 
female-type sex differentiation of XX gonads (Fig. 3c). We introduced 
a mutant mouse line carrying an Hsp-Sry transgene14 into this experi-
ment to force expression of Sry; this restored male-type sex differen-
tiation (Fig. 3c), indicating that the lack of endogenous Sry expression 
was the cause of male-to-female sex reversal in DFO-treated gonads. 
When sufficient iron was added in combination with DFO treatment, 
male-type gonadal sex differentiation was completely restored (Fig. 3c), 
suggesting that the sex reversal associated with by DFO treatment was 
due to iron deficiency.
To further investigate how iron depletion influences the gene- 
expression networks that underpin gonadal sex determination, 
DFO-treated NR5A1+ cells were isolated and analysed by mRNA-seq 
(Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 1). The gene-expression profiles of 
XY gonadal somatic cells in in-vitro-cultured gonads were distinct from 
those developed in utero, possibly owing to the different developing 
conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3d); however, the expression levels of 
genes related to early gonadogenesis and/or Sry regulation were not 
influenced by in vitro culture experiments (Extended Data Fig. 3e). 
Notably, Sry expression was markedly decreased in DFO-treated NR5A1+ 
cells, to around one-fifth that in untreated NR5A1+ cells (Fig. 3d and 
Extended Data Fig. 3e). These findings indicate that DFO treatment 
affects the gene networks for male gonadal sex determination directly 
at the point of Sry expression, consistent with the role of KDM3A in 
these gene networks1. Approximately 40% of KDM3A target genes, 
including Sry, were downregulated by DFO treatment (Extended Data 
Fig. 3f), supporting the hypothesis that iron deficiency during gonadal 
development compromises KDM3A activity.
We found that the expression of the iron-incorporation gene Tfrc and 
the Fe2+-production gene Hmox1 was upregulated by DFO treatment 
(Fig. 3d). Of note, the expression of a set of iron-requiring epigenetic 
modifier genes, including Kdm3a, was upregulated by DFO treatment 
(Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 3g,h), suggesting a possible feedback 
regulation of the gene expression of these enzymes according to iron 
levels.
We next evaluated the effect of DFO treatment on histone modifica-
tion in in-vitro-cultured gonads. When cultured in control medium, 
the levels of H3K9me2 were obviously lower in gonadal somatic cells 
than in mesonephric cells (Fig. 3e). However, when cultured with DFO, 
H3K9me2 in gonadal somatic cells increased to levels comparable 
with those in mesonephric cells (Fig. 3e). Quantitative immunoblot 
analysis indicated that the levels of H3K9me2 in DFO-treated NR5A1+ 
cells were almost double those in untreated NR5A1+ cells, in both XY and 
XX gonads (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 3i). Conversely, the levels of 
unmethylated H3K9 in DFO-treated NR5A1+ cells were nearly half those 
in untreated NR5A1+ cells (Fig. 3f). ChIP–qPCR analysis showed that 
the levels of H3K9me2 at the Sry promoter in DFO-treated NR5A1+ cells 
were also almost double those in untreated NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data 
Fig. 3j). We found that H3K9me2 levels at the canonical KDM3A target 
genes were also increased by DFO treatment (Extended Data Fig. 3j), 
again supporting the conclusion that KDM3A activity is compromised 
by DFO treatment.
To address whether the reduced H3K9 demethylation was the sole 
cause of Sry suppression in DFO-treated gonads, we used genetic and 
chemical approaches. We previously showed that the EHMT1–EHMT2 
H3K9 dimethyltransferase complex antagonizes KDM3A-mediated 
H3K9 demethylation at the Sry locus; introduction of a heterozygous 
mutation of Ehmt1 into a Kdm3a-deficient background resulted in 
reduced levels of H3K9me2 at the Sry locus and restored Sry expression 
in embryonic gonads2. As shown in Fig. 3g, averaged SRY expression in 
DFO-treated XY gonads was around 30% of that in untreated XY gonads. 
However, when XY Ehmt1Δ/+ gonads were cultured with DFO, SRY expres-
sion was restored to nearly 50% of that in the untreated control (Fig. 3g). 
RK-701 is a chemical inhibitor of the EHMT1–EHMT2 complex15. We 
found that SRY expression was restored by adding RK-701 during DFO 
treatment, to nearly 70% of that in the untreated control (Fig. 3g).

were also restored by introducing a heterozygous mutation of Ehmt1 
and by adding RK-701 (Fig. 3h). These results together confirm that 
iron-deficiency-induced suppression of Sry is caused by the absence 
of H3K9 demethylation at the Sry locus. Because JmjC-family H3K9 
demethylases other than Kdm3a were also expressed in NR5A1+ cells

Maternal iron deficiency causes fetal sex reversal
We next tested whether maternal iron deficiency influences the sex 
development of embryos in utero. First, we pharmaceutically induced 
maternal iron deficiency around the time of embryonic sex determi-
nation, by administering the oral iron chelator deferasirox (DFX)16 to 
pregnant mothers daily from E6.5 to E10.5, and then examined the sex 
development of developing embryos in utero (Fig. 4a). E11.5 embryos 
carried by DFX-treated mothers exhibited typical anaemia; their bod-
ies were pale in colour (Fig. 4a), and the levels of H- and L-ferritin were 
markedly decreased in their NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a).
Of 72 XY mice born to DFX-treated mothers, four had two ovaries 
and one had an ovary and a testis (Fig. 4b), indicating that acute 
maternal iron deficiency around the sex-determining period results 
in male-to-female sex reversal in a proportion of the wild-type offspring.
Because the number of NR5A1+ cells in E11.5 gonads was indistinguish-
able between XY embryos carried by DFX-treated mothers and those 
carried by control mothers, DFX did not affect the growth potential 
of embryonic gonadal somatic cells (Extended Data Fig. 4b). On the 
other hand, SRY expression was profoundly decreased in XY gonads 
of embryos carried by DFX-treated mothers, to nearly 60% of that in 
control XY gonads (Fig. 4c). Sry mRNA expression was decreased in 
NR5A1+ cells in XY gonads of embryos carried by DFX-treated mothers, 
to nearly 40% of that in control NR5A1+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). As 
well as the in-vitro-cultured gonads shown in Fig. 3d, iron deficiency 
induced the upregulation of Kdm3a and iron-metabolism genes and 
the downregulation of KDM3A target genes in NR5A1+ cells in embryos 
developed in utero (Extended Data Fig. 4c). These data suggest that 
maternal iron deficiency intrinsically influences the activation of Sry 
(and SRY) in developing embryos in utero, at least in part through inhib-
iting KDM3A activity.
We examined how treating mothers with DFX influences embryonic 
gonadal sex differentiation, and found that E13.5 XY gonads in embryos 
carried by DFX-treated mothers had typical ovotestes that contained 
both FOXL2+ cells and SOX9+ cells, with the proportion of FOXL2+ cells 
reaching about 20% (Fig. 4d). Restoring the function of SRY through 
forced expression of the Hsp-Sry transgene effectively reduced the pro-
portion of FOXL2+ cells in XY gonads of embryos carried by DFX-treated 
mothers to nearly that seen in XY control gonads (Fig. 4d), indicat-
ing that the ovotestis phenotype of XY gonads in embryos carried by 
DFX-treated mothers was due to reduced expression of Sry (SRY).
Finally, to evaluate whether a reduction in the maternal dietary intake 
of iron might influence the sex development of developing embryos, 
we fed female mice an iron-deficient diet (IDD) over a period of six 
weeks, including four weeks before pregnancy (Fig. 5a). In the moth-
ers, IDD treatment progressively reduced the levels of haemoglobin 
and the number of red blood cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a), and anae-
mia was observed when the corresponding embryos had reached the

to the gonads in embryos carried by IDD-fed mothers as IDD gonads, and 
those in embryos carried by mothers that were fed a control diet (CD) 
as CD gonads. Cellular iron levels in E11.5 NR5A1+ cells in IDD gonads 
were around 60% of those in CD gonads (Fig. 5b). Fetal iron deficiency 
was confirmed by protein expression analysis: TFR1 was increased, and 
H- and L-ferritin were decreased, in E11.5 NR5A1+ cells in IDD gonads, 
compared with those in CD gonads (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Again, the 
number of NR5A1+ cells was indistinguishable between IDD gonads 
and CD gonads (Extended Data Fig. 5d). As shown in Fig. 5c, we found 
that wild-type XY postnatal offspring (n = 58) born to IDD-fed mothers 
developed normally.

and canalized, such that some perturbations do not readily manifest 
as sex reversal17–20. A sensitized genetic background is thus a com-
mon strategy for assaying the phenotypic effects of perturbations of 
sex-determining pathways1,21. We therefore repeated the experiment 
using embryos heterozygous for a mutation in Kdm3a (Kdm3aΔ/+), which

are phenotypically normal but sensitized to compromised H3K9 dem-
ethylation. With the Kdm3aΔ/+ embryos, 2 of 43 XY offspring born to 
IDD-fed mothers showed male-to-female sex reversal, whereas none of 
the offspring (n = 60) born to CD-fed mothers showed this phenotype 
(Fig. 5c). Examination of gonadal sex differentiation in E13.5 embryos 
showed that FOXL2+ cells emerged in Kdm3a+/+ IDD gonads, and that 
this population was more numerous in Kdm3aΔ/+ IDD gonads (Fig. 5d). 
These data indicate that maternal dietary iron deficiency can act as a 
factor that induces male-to-female sex reversal in mammalian fetuses 
with a certain genetic background.
We investigated the cellular and molecular effects of maternal iron 
status on fetal gonadal development. SRY expression was decreased in 
XY Kdm3a+/+ IDD gonads, to nearly 70% of that in XY Kdm3a+/+ CD gonads 
(Fig. 5e). We found that SRY expression was further decreased in E11.5 
XY Kdm3aΔ/+ gonads, to nearly 50% of that in XY Kdm3a+/+ CD gonads 
(Fig. 5e). Among the different genotypic and dietary conditions of XY 
developing gonads, gonadal H3K9me2 levels were found to be highest 
in Kdm3aΔ/+ IDD gonads, followed by Kdm3a+/+ IDD gonads and then 
Kdm3a+/+ CD gonads (Fig. 5f). These data support the notion that the 
point of action of maternal dietary iron deficiency is KDM3A-mediated 
Sry activation.
As summarized in Fig. 5g, iron-incorporating and Fe2+-producing 
pathways are simultaneously activated in developing gonads during sex 
determination, thereby facilitating KDM3A-mediated H3K9 demethyla-
tion at the Sry locus. Because this epigenetic regulation of Sry is highly 
dependent on intracellular Fe2+ levels, maternal iron deficiency causes 
male-to-female sex reversal in some developing embryos in utero.
Discussion
Our studies indicate that intracellular iron levels act as a crucial rate- 
limiting factor for H3K9 demethylation in developing gonads. In vitro 
culture analyses showed that reducing intracellular iron to 40% of 
control levels led to a massive increase in H3K9me2 at the Sry locus, 
and mostly abolished Sry expression. We therefore deduce that the 
threshold level of gonadal iron required for male sex determination is 
approximately 40% of that in the wild type. Because high expression of 
the H3K9 methyltransferase EHMT1–EHMT2 complex catalyses H3K9 
methylation at the Sry locus in E11.5 gonadal somatic cells2, it seems 
likely that H3K9me2-abundant heterochromatin is a default charac-
teristic of the Sry locus. To overcome heterochromatinization of the 
Sry locus during the sex-determining period, not only the expression 
of KDM3A, but also the production of the essential cofactor Fe2+, must 
be upregulated.
We found an inverse correlation between cellular iron levels and 
Kdm3a expression in gonadal somatic cells, indicating a possible 
feedback system between iron levels and the expression of Kdm3a. 
It is well known that iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) are important for 
mRNA stabilization: in iron-deficient conditions, binding of IRPs to 
iron-responsive elements (IREs) of the 3′ untranslated region (3′-UTR) 
confers iron-dependent stabilization on the mRNA22,23. However, 
because we could not find IREs in the 3′-UTR of Kdm3a, the upregula-
tion of Kdm3a might be independent of the IRP–IRE system. It is known 
that the transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) is 
stabilized when intracellular iron availability decreases. HIF1α binds 
to the Kdm3a promoter and induces its expression in several tumour 
cell lines24–26. It is plausible that iron-deficiency-induced upregulation 
of Kdm3a might be regulated by HIF1α in developing gonads.
Other than KDM3A, nearly 20 genes encoding JmjC-domain- 
containing histone demethylases exist in the mammalian genome, 
which also require Fe2+ for their demethylating activity. Histone methyl-
ation is involved in both gene suppression and gene activation, depend-
ing on the lysine residues to be methylated (for example, H3K9 and 
H3K27 methylation for suppression and H3K4 and H3K36 methylation 
for activation). In addition, TET enzymes, which are involved in DNA 
demethylation pathways, also require Fe2+ for their activity. It will be 
worth investigating how iron deficiency alters gene-expression profiles 
during developmental process other than gonadal sex determination, 
by altering histone and DNA methylation status.
In summary, we show that pharmaceutical suppression of available 
iron, or feeding pregnant mice a low-iron diet, results in changes to 
epigenetic status in developing mouse embryos in utero, impairs the 
activation of Sry in XY embryonic gonads and causes male-to-female 
sex reversal in a proportion of mouse embryos. Iron deficiency during 
pregnancy affects an estimated 35.5% of pregnant women (https://www.
who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/anaemia_in_women_and_chil-
dren). Furthermore, Diamond–Blackfan and Fanconi anaemia have 
been reported as risk factors for 46,XY disorders of sex development 
in humans27,28. Our findings now establish a role for iron in mammalian 
sex determination and highlight the potential importance of maintain-
ing adequate iron levels in pregnant mothers—particularly those who 
might be at risk of iron deficiency—to ensure proper sex differentiation 
in the fetus.

===== Bower2025_Nature_RangeExtender-Enhancer =====

830  |  Nature  |  Vol 643  |  17 July 2025

Range extender mediates long-distance 
enhancer activity
Grace Bower1, Ethan W. Hollingsworth1,2, Sandra H. Jacinto1, Joshua A. Alcantara1, 
Benjamin Clock1, Kaitlyn Cao1, Mandy Liu1, Adam Dziulko3, Ana Alcaina-Caro4, Qianlan Xu5,6,7, 
Dorota Skowronska-Krawczyk5,6,7, Javier Lopez-Rios4,8, Diane E. Dickel3,13, Anaïs F. Bardet9, 
Len A. Pennacchio3,10,11, Axel Visel3,10,12 & Evgeny Z. Kvon1 ✉
Although most mammalian transcriptional enhancers regulate their cognate 
promoters over distances of tens of kilobases, some enhancers act over distances  
in the megabase range1. The sequence features that enable such long-distance 
enhancer–promoter interactions remain unclear. Here we used in vivo enhancer- 
replacement experiments at the mouse Shh locus to show that short- and medium- 
range limb enhancers cannot initiate gene expression at long-distance range. We 
identify a cis-acting element, range extender (REX), that confers long-distance 
regulatory activity and is located next to a long-range limb enhancer of Sall1. The  
REX element has no endogenous enhancer activity. However, addition of the REX to 
other short- and mid-range limb enhancers substantially increases their genomic 
interaction range. In the most extreme example observed, addition of REX increased 
the range of an enhancer by an order of magnitude from its native 73 kb to 848 kb.  
The REX element contains highly conserved [C/T]AATTA homeodomain motifs that 
are critical for its activity. These motifs are enriched in long-range limb enhancers 
genome-wide, including the ZRS (zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) regulatory 
sequence), a benchmark long-range limb enhancer of Shh2. The ZRS enhancer with 
mutated [C/T]AATTA motifs maintains limb activity at short range, but loses its 
long-range activity, resulting in severe limb reduction in knock-in mice. In summary, 
we identify a sequence signature associated with long-range enhancer–promoter 
interactions and describe a prototypical REX element that is necessary and sufficient 
to confer long-distance activation by remote enhancers.
Transcriptional enhancers are abundant cis-acting non-coding genomic 
elements that activate gene expression across different cell types of 
the organism in response to internal and external signals3–7. Enhanc-
ers often regulate their target promoters across long genomic dis-
tances1,2,8–10. Disruption of this long-range gene regulation often leads 
to diseases ranging from developmental anomalies to cancer8,11–14.
A central question in gene regulation is how remote enhancers pre-
cisely relay regulatory information to their target promoters located 
hundreds of thousands or even millions of base pairs away, often with-
out affecting the expression of intervening genes. Enhancers come into 
physical proximity to activate target promoters, but the mechanisms 
that mediate these functionally important interactions are only par-
tially understood1,15. Mounting evidence indicates that higher-order 
three-dimensional (3D) chromatin organization and structural CTCF 
and cohesin proteins support enhancer–promoter (E–P) interactions 
by restricting E–P communication to topologically associating domains 
(TADs)16–20. However, the global disruption of higher-order 3D chroma-
tin organization and loop extrusion in CTCF- and cohesin-depleted cells 
only partially impairs E–P communication and gene expression21–25. Fur-
thermore, developmental gene expression is also surprisingly robust 
to CTCF-binding-site deletions and structural perturbations affecting 
TADs26–31. Thus, which additional genetic factors establish and main-
tain long-range E–P communication during mammalian development 
remains poorly understood1,13,15,32. Identifying such factors is crucial for 
achieving an in-depth understanding of developmental processes and 
delineating disease mechanisms linked to disruption of long-range 
gene regulation.
Here we identify a unique sequence signature comprising [C/T]
AATTA homeodomain (HD) motifs that mediates long-range E–P com-
munication in developing limb buds. Deletion of these motifs selectively

abolishes distal enhancer activity but not its short-range ability. The 
[C/T]AATTA motifs are enriched at long-distance limb enhancer loci 
genome-wide and their presence correlates with E–P distance. We 
also characterize an extreme case in which the [C/T]AATTA motifs 
are located spatially separate from the enhancer within a genomic 
element, which we termed the REX element. The addition of the REX 
element can convert a short-range enhancer into a long-range enhancer 
that can act over 848 kb of genomic space. Our results indicate that 
short- or medium-range enhancers cannot function at long-distance 
range and establish that spatial specificity and long-distance activity 
are two separate and separable aspects of enhancer function.
Medium-range enhancers cannot act at long range
To test the potential of short- and medium-range enhancers to act over 
long genomic distances, we performed a series of enhancer-replacement 
experiments at the Shh genomic locus. Limb-specific expression of Shh 
is controlled by the ZRS (also known as MFCS1), located at an extreme 
distance of about 848 kb from its target promoter in mice2. Mice defi-
cient for the ZRS do not initiate any Shh expression in developing limb 
buds and display truncated limb phenotypes that are indistinguishable 
from those of mice with complete loss of SHH function in the limb33. 
Owing to the clear phenotypic readout and lack of redundancy, ZRS-Shh 
is an ideal locus for assessing the long-range enhancer activity of trans-
planted enhancers.
To perform enhancer-replacement experiments, we selected four 
previously characterized developmental limb enhancers from other 
genomic loci on the basis of their ability to drive robust LacZ reporter 
expression in the developing limb bud mesenchyme (MM1492 and 
MM1564 (from mouse) and HS1516 and HS72 (from human); Fig. 1a,b). 
The HS72, HS1516 and MM1492 enhancers also drive LacZ reporter 
expression in the ZPA, a posterior domain of the limb mesenchyme 
where ZRS activates Shh gene expression (Fig. 1b). All four enhancers 
are evolutionarily conserved and marked by acetylation at lysine 27 
in histone H3 (H3K27ac) in limb buds, a histone modification that is 
associated with active enhancers (Fig. 1a). To determine the genomic 
distance at which these enhancers act on their native promoters and 
to ensure that they are accessible to transcription factors (TFs) in the 
same cell types as the ZRS, we performed single-nucleus assay for 
transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (snATAC–seq) 
and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) multiome profil-
ing of 14,000 cells from a wild-type (WT) embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5) 
hindlimb bud (Methods). After clustering all 14,000 cells on the basis of 
their chromatin and gene expression profiles, we annotated 16 clusters 
representing all major cell types in the developing limb bud (Methods, 
Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). The HS72, HS1516 and

Article
MM1492 enhancers display strong DNA accessibility in Shh positive ZPA 
cells, consistent with their ability to drive robust reporter expression 
in posterior limb mesenchyme in transgenic mouse embryos (Fig. 1a).
To link limb enhancers to their putative target genes, we used the 
correlation between gene expression and open chromatin peaks 
from multiome profiling and E–P physical interaction data based on 
tissue-resolved high-resolution enhancer-capture Hi-C experiments 
(Methods). We identified Prdm16 as the target for MM1492 (73 kb away), 
Ets2 as the target for mHS1516 (mouse homologue of HS1516) (147 kb 
away) and Sall1 as the target for mHS72 (mouse homologue of HS72) 
(411 kb away) (Fig. 1c). We then manually matched enhancer activity 
and the expression patterns of genes located within the same TADs in 
E11.5 mouse embryos. This analysis confirmed the above E–P links and 
additionally identified Rbms1 as a putative target for MM1564 (177 kb 
away; Fig. 1b,c).
We next used genome editing to create a series of knock-in (KI) mice 
in which the functionally critical 1.3-kb region of the ZRS (Fig. 1d and 
Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) was replaced with selected limb bud enhanc-
ers from other genomic loci. Notably, replacing the mouse ZRS with 
HS72, MM1564, HS1516 or MM1492 limb enhancers resulted in a loss of 
detectable Shh expression in the limb bud (Fig. 1e). To assess the extent 
to which replacing the ZRS with a heterologous limb enhancer affects 
in vivo development, we examined the skeletal morphology in E18.5 
KI mice. Consistent with the loss of limb-specific Shh expression, all 
four KI mouse strains displayed a truncated limb phenotype affecting 
both the forelimbs and hindlimbs. The limb phenotypes were indistin-
guishable from the phenotype caused by replacement of the ZRS with a 
nonfunctional control sequence of similar length (Fig. 1e and Extended 
Data Fig. 2c). These results indicate that, despite the presence of bona 
fide enhancer features capable of driving strong limb gene expression 
in the context of a transgene, all four enhancers lack long-range activity 
and cannot support Shh-mediated limb development.
Transplanted enhancers are accessible
It is possible that silencing of the inserted region or failure of the inser-
tions to create an open chromatin environment explains the inability of 
transplanted regions to act as long-range enhancers34,35. To test whether 
enhancers maintain their endogenous chromatin architecture at a 
remote ectopic location, we performed ATAC–seq experiments in ZPA 
region of forelimb and hindlimb buds of E11.5 mice heterozygous for 
the ZRSHS72 and ZRSHS1516 KI alleles.
HS72 and HS1516 are human enhancers that are highly conserved in 
mice but contain substitutions that allow discrimination of ATAC–seq 
reads from transplanted human and orthologous endogenous mouse 
enhancers (Methods and Extended Data Fig. 3). ZRSHS72 and ZRSHS1516 
heterozygous mice formed normal limbs (Extended Data Fig. 2d), 
which enabled us to directly compare chromatin accessibility at the 
transplanted enhancer allele and the WT ZRS enhancer allele in fully 
developed limb bud tissue of the same mouse. Allele-specific ATAC–seq 
profiles demonstrated that both transplanted enhancers and ortholo-
gous mouse enhancers had an accessible open chromatin architecture 
(Fig. 2a). These results indicate that the heterologous HS72 and HS1516 
limb enhancers were accessible when transplanted, but were unable 
to activate gene expression remotely, further supporting the idea that 
their inability to activate the Shh promoter in ZRS-replacement experi-
ments is due to limitations in their genomic interaction range.
The HS72 enhancer activates Shh at short range
The inability of heterologous limb enhancers to activate Shh expression 
was surprising, given their robust enhancer features and ability to estab-
lish open chromatin at the transplanted location. Previously, all four limb 
enhancers were characterized in transgenic mice using a well-established 
hsp68 minimal promoter, but their compatibility with the Shh promoter 
is unclear. To test whether E–P incompatibility36,37 could have a role in the 
observed differences in gene activation, we placed the HS72 enhancer 
upstream of the mouse Shh promoter and the LacZ reporter gene and 
injected the resulting construct into fertilized mouse eggs. All transgenic 
mouse embryos (7 out of 7) displayed strong LacZ expression in the limb 
buds, which was identical to HS72’s activity with the hsp68 promoter, 
indicating that the HS72 enhancer is fully capable of activating the Shh 
promoter (Figs. 1a and 2b). Moreover, we previously showed that 32 
enhancers characterised with the hsp68 promoter maintained their 
in vivo activity when tested with the Shh promoter38–40.
To test whether the HS72 enhancer can activate gene expression at 
the endogenous Shh locus, we generated a KI line in which the HS72 
enhancer sequence was inserted around 2 kb upstream of the endog-
enous Shh promoter (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Preaxial 
polydactyly (formation of extra digits) provides a sensitive and readily 
accessible phenotypic readout of ectopic Shh misexpression beyond 
the ZPA of the developing limb2,41. As HS72 is active more broadly than 
the ZRS in limb mesenchyme, the presence of polydactyly would indi-
cate that it can activate functional SHH signalling. Indeed, ShhHS72(+2kb)/WT 
mice had polydactylous forelimbs and hindlimbs and de novo Shh 
expression in anterior hindlimb buds consistent with the HS72 enhancer 
driving expanded Shh activity42 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4b). 
This result was similar to the polydactyly observed in transgenic mice 
in which the HS72::Shh transgene was integrated at a safe-harbour 
location in the mouse genome (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Importantly, 
ZRSHS72/WT mice had normal limbs, indicating the absence of broad 
HS72-mediated Shh activation from a remote position (Extended Data 
Fig. 2d). Together, these results show that the HS72 enhancer can acti-
vate the Shh promoter at short range in its native endogenous context 
and in the context of a transgene.
REX is required for long-range activation
The HS72 enhancer is compatible with the Shh promoter and is acces-
sible when transplanted in place of the ZRS (Fig. 2) suggesting that its 
failure to activate Shh remotely could be due to the extreme distance 
from the Shh promoter. Indeed, the HS72, MM1564, HS1516 and MM1492 
enhancers lie closer to their putative target genes than the ZRS (Fig. 1c). 
We hypothesized that there may be additional functional sequences 
associated with distant-acting enhancers that support long-range acti-
vation. To explore possible missing factors in long-distance activa-
tion, we examined the genomic region proximal to the HS72 enhancer, 
which has the longest native activity range among four heterologous 
enhancers at 411 kb away from the Sall1 promoter (Fig. 1c). We identi-
fied a highly conserved block of sequence located adjacent to the HS72 
enhancer (Fig. 3a). This sequence is not required to drive limb-specific 
activity in reporter assays (Figs. 1b and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4), 
but, owing to its strong conservation and position, we hypothesized 
that this sequence might support enhancer activity, including the 
ability to activate gene expression over remote distances. To test this 
hypothesis, we generated KI mice in which the ZRS was replaced with 
an extended version of the HS72 enhancer that included this highly 
conserved upstream sequence (Fig. 3b).
Consistent with our prediction, addition of this uncharacterized 
sequence, which we termed the REX element, to the transplanted 
HS72 enhancer was sufficient to initiate Shh expression in the limb and 
resulted in full limb outgrowth with formation of all distal limb elements 
including fully formed zeugopod and autopod in ZRSHS72+REX/HS72+REX 
mice (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 5a). ZRSHS72+REX/HS72+REX mice also 
displayed polydactyly on both forelimbs and hindlimbs, consistent with 
ectopic Shh expression in limb buds driven by broader HS72 enhancer 
activity (Figs. 1b and 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c).
Notably, the REX element alone does not act as a classical enha­
ncer. When placed upstream of the minimal promoter in a transgene, 
it is unable to drive LacZ reporter expression in transgenic mouse 

Nature  |  Vol 643  |  17 July 2025  |  833
embryos (Fig. 3c). Together, these results indicate that the REX element 
does not have enhancer activity on its own but is required for long-range 
heterologous enhancer activation at the Shh locus.
REX is sufficient for long-range activation
To test whether the REX element can extend the range of heterologous 
short-range enhancers, we generated a KI mouse line in which the ZRS 
was replaced with a chimeric element consisting of the shortest-range 
heterologous limb enhancer from our test set (MM1492, 73 kb native 
E—P range) appended by the REX element (MM1492 + REX; Extended 
Data Fig. 5d). KI of this chimeric element was sufficient to induce Shh 
expression in the limb bud and resulted in a fully developed zeugopod 
and autopod in the ZRSMM1492+REX/MM1492+REX mice (Fig. 3d and Extended Data 
Fig. 5e). These mice also displayed polydactyly, consistent with broad 
limb activity of MM1492. Taken together, these experiments show that 
combining a short-range enhancer with the REX element and placing 
them at an ectopic remote location is sufficient to induce long-range 
gene activation. These results also suggest that the REX element can 
act in a modular manner to facilitate long-range enhancer action.
LHX motifs are critical for REX activity
To identify specific TFs that may be involved in REX-mediated 
long-range enhancer action, we examined potential TF-binding sites 
within the REX element. The REX element lacks CTCF and YY1 motifs and 
is not bound by CTCF in embryonic limb buds (Extended Data Fig. 6j). 
We scanned the REX element sequence for other candidate TF-binding 
sites and identified conserved motifs of which the sequences matched 
binding preferences for LHX2 and LHX9 homeodomain (HD) TFs as 
well as LEF1 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6a).
To determine the importance of LHX and LEF1 motifs for REX func-
tion, we generated two KI mice in which the ZRS was replaced with the 
extended HS72 sequence containing the REX element with either the

REX element with mutated LEF1 motif showed fully developed limbs

LHX motifs are enriched in remote enhancers
To investigate whether the LHX or other TF motifs are present at long- 
range limb enhancers, we used a collection of experimentally validated 
limb enhancers from the VISTA Enhancer Browser, a unique resource 
of human and mouse enhancers with in vivo activities characterized 
in transgenic mice43. We linked these bona fide limb enhancers to their 
putative target genes using the correlation between gene expression 
and open chromatin peaks from our single-cell ATAC–seq (scATAC–
seq) and scRNA-seq experiment or E–P physical interactions from 
enhancer-capture Hi-C experiments (Extended Data Fig. 1d). We next 
performed motif analysis of these limb enhancers. We found 33 motifs 
that match the binding preferences of limb-expressed TFs that are 
significantly enriched in long-range acting (173 regions; E–P distance, 
400 kb to 2 Mb) compared to short-range acting (28 regions; E–P dis-
tance, 10–200 kb) enhancer regions (false-discovery-rate-adjusted 
P < 1 × 10−2 and target frequency > 30%), with LHX2 and LHX9 being

and Supplementary Table 2). Overall, HD TFs with a similar [C/T]AATTA 
consensus binding preference, including DLX5, MSX2 and SHOX2, com-
prised 10 out of these 33 motifs. By contrast, short-range limb enhanc-
ers showed no enrichment for TF motifs over long-range enhancers.
We next examined all 19,276 limb mesenchyme E–P pairs predicted 
from our scATAC–seq/scRNA-seq experiment (Extended Data Fig. 6c 
and Supplementary Table 2). Genome wide, the LHX2 motif was among 
the most significantly enriched in long-range versus short-range limb 
enhancers (CTAATTA, P < 6 × 10−32). Overall, [C/T]AATTA HD motifs, 
including both LHX2 and LHX9 motifs, comprised 15 out of the top 
20 most significantly enriched motifs in long-range limb enhancers.
The REX element contains two conserved LHX [C/T]AATTA motifs 
located within 30 bp from each other that are required for long range 
enhancer activity (Fig. 4a,c). To test whether having more than one [C/T]
AATTA motif could be characteristic of other long-range enhancers, 
we examined the number of [C/T]AATTA motifs in experimentally 
validated and multiome-predicted limb enhancers (Methods). Indeed, 
for limb enhancers containing more than one [C/T]AATTA motif the 
enhancer regions were on average 429 kb farther (median distance) 
from their target promoters than other limb enhancers (P < 0.01; Fig. 4e 
and Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Taken together, these results indicate that 
conserved [C/T]AATTA HD motifs are enriched in long-distance limb 
enhancers throughout the genome and are frequently located within 
the conserved core of enhancers themselves (Extended Data Fig. 6k).

To test their requirement for spatiotemporal limb-specific ZRS activ-
ity, we used dual-enSERT, our recently developed dual-fluorescence 
reporter system that enables comparison of enhancer allele activi-
ties in the same mouse44. We generated a construct in which a WT 
approximately 1.3 kb mouse ZRS drives mCherry and the same ZRS 
allele but with mutated [C/T]AATTA HD motifs (ZRSΔHD), drives eGFP. 
The transgenes were separated by a synthetic insulator to prevent 
reporter gene cross-activation. We left all other TF-binding sites that 
were previously shown to be important for ZRS enhancer activity intact, 
including ETS1, ETV, HOX and E-BOX motifs (Fig. 5a). We injected the 
resulting ZRS–mCherry/ZRSΔHD–eGFP bicistronic construct into 
mouse zygotes and collected transgenic embryos at E11.5. We detected 
mCherry and eGFP fluorescence in the ZPA, indicating that the ZRS 
enhancer lacking [C/T]AATTA motifs can act over short range and drive 
robust reporter expression (Fig. 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). 
We obtained a similar result when we swapped fluorescent reporter 
genes, ruling out the influence of fluorophores on our observations 
(Fig. 5c). While both the ZRS and ZRSΔHD directed expression in a 
spatially highly restricted manner to the ZPA, ZRSΔHD showed lower, 
albeit not statistically significant, quantitative activity than the ZRS 
regardless of the fluorescent reporter pairing. This may be due to the 
close proximity of [C/T]AATTA HD motifs to the ETS sites, which are 
critical for ZRS activity45. Importantly, we observed only mCherry 
expression and no detectable eGFP expression in transgenic mice lack-
ing enhancer upstream of the eGFP, indicating that there is no reporter 
cross-activation (P < 0.0182; Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 7b).

these motifs are required for long-distance E–P communication. We 
created a KI mouse line in which we disrupted the same three [C/T]
AATTA motifs within the endogenous ZRS enhancer region. Notably,

outgrowth indistinguishable from complete loss of SHH function in 
the limb consistent with the specific requirement of [C/T]AATTA motifs 
for long-range ZRS activity (Figs. 1d and 5d). The loss of limb outgrowth 
in ZRS∆HD/∆HD mice could be almost completely rescued by addition of 
the REX element; mice containing the ZRSΔHD allele fused to the REX 
element fully developed zeugopod and part of the autopod with four 
digits on both forelimbs and hindlimbs (Fig. 5e).
Taken together, our KI and transgenic results indicate that [C/T]
AATTA HD motifs in the ZRS are dispensable for limb-specific activity 
at short range, but are critically required for long-range activity. These 
experiments uncouple the marked tissue specificity of the ZRS, direct-
ing highly restricted expression to the ZPA, from its ability to act over 
extremely long genomic distances. Our results also indicate that the loss 
of long-range enhancer activity after the removal of endogenous [C/T]
AATTA HD motifs could be compensated by addition of a heterologous 
REX element, demonstrating that the [C/T]AATTA HD motifs found in 
the REX element and the ZRS are functionally equivalent.
Discussion
Here we have identified an evolutionarily conserved signature that is 
specifically required to confer long-distance E–P communication at 
the Shh genomic locus. We also describe a prototypical element con-
taining this signature, REX, that is sufficient to confer long-distance 
interactivity to heterologous short- and medium-range limb enhancers. 
This finding reveals a fundamental aspect of enhancer function that 
cannot be measured in traditional transgenic reporter experiments 
and provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for previous observa-
tions that linear distance can impact an enhancer’s ability to activate 
gene expression46–48.
Cis-regulatory elements that facilitate enhancer activity con-
tinue to emerge as essential regulators of gene expression. This list 
includes Drosophila tethering49–51 and remote control elements52 
along with mammalian CTCF sites28,53–57, CpG islands58 and facilitator 
elements59,60. The REX element adds to this list but it does not share 
sequence similarity with any of the previously described elements. 
Both the REX element and the ZRS enhancer contain highly conserved 
[C/T]AATTA-binding sites that are required for long-range activa-
tion. Our experiments showing the preferential requirement of [C/T]
AATTA motifs for long- but not short-range enhancer activity suggest 
that their cognate TFs could specifically mediate long-range E–P 
activation but may not be critical for general transcriptional activa-
tion. The [C/T]AATTA motifs match the binding preferences of many 
HD TFs, notably the LIM-HD TFs LHX2 and LHX9 that are required for 
normal limb outgrowth61,62. Indeed, LIM-domain-associated TFs such 
as GATA1, ISL1 and LHX2 are known to facilitate E–P looping at the 
β-globin locus as well as the assembly of interchromosomal olfactory 
gene compartments through their cofactor LIM-domain-binding fac-
tor (LDB1)63–66. However, their general role in regulating long-range 
E–P interactions is currently an area of open investigation67,68. Global 
enrichment of [C/T]AATTA HD motifs in long-distance enhancers sug-
gests that there are probably more REX elements across the genome, 
with many of them integrated into the enhancer itself, as we showed 
with the ZRS (Fig. 5f).
As our enhancer-substitution experiments were performed at the Shh 
locus, we cannot rule out the potential impact of locus-specific effects 
on our findings. Further investigation into long- versus short-range 
enhancer activity at other genomic loci and across different cell types 
will be necessary to understand how widespread REX elements are 
in mammalian genomes and to dissect the molecular mechanism of 
REX element function. Nevertheless, our results suggest that cell-type 
specificity and long-range activity are two distinct aspects of gene 
activation by enhancers, probably fulfilled by separate sets of TFs. 
This separation will have implications for interpretation of human 
genetics studies as some non-coding variants will probably affect only 
long-range enhancer ability while others will disrupt cell-type-specific 
gene activation.

Cryptic variation fuels plant phenotypic 
change through hierarchical epistasis
Sophia G. Zebell1,2, Carlos Martí-Gómez1, Blaine Fitzgerald1,2, Camila P. Cunha3, Michael Lach3, 
Brooke M. Seman1,2, Anat Hendelman1,2, Simon Sretenovic4,6, Yiping Qi4, Madelaine Bartlett5, 
Yuval Eshed3 ✉, David M. McCandlish1 ✉ & Zachary B. Lippman1,2 ✉
Cryptic genetic variants exert minimal phenotypic effects alone but are hypothesized 
to form a vast reservoir of genetic diversity driving trait evolvability through epistatic 
interactions1–3. This classical theory has been reinvigorated by pan-genomics, which  
is revealing pervasive variation within gene families, cis-regulatory regions and 
regulatory networks4–6. Testing the ability of cryptic variation to fuel phenotypic 
diversification has been hindered by intractable genetics, limited allelic diversity  
and inadequate phenotypic resolution. Here, guided by natural and engineered 
cis-regulatory cryptic variants in a paralogous gene pair, we identified additional 
redundant trans regulators, establishing a regulatory network controlling tomato 
inflorescence architecture. By combining coding mutations with cis-regulatory alleles 
in populations segregating for all four network genes, we generated 216 genotypes 
spanning a wide spectrum of inflorescence complexity and quantified branching in 
over 35,000 inflorescences. Analysis of this high-resolution genotype–phenotype map 
using a hierarchical model of epistasis revealed a layer of dose-dependent interactions 
within paralogue pairs enhancing branching, culminating in strong, synergistic effects. 
However, we also identified a layer of antagonism between paralogue pairs, whereby 
accumulating mutations in one pair progressively diminished the effects of mutations 
in the other. Our results demonstrate how gene regulatory network architecture and 
complex dosage effects from paralogue diversification converge to shape phenotypic 
space, producing the potential for both strongly buffered phenotypes and sudden 
bursts of phenotypic change.
An enduring debate in evolutionary biology concerns the extent to 
which small-effect genetic variants contribute to expanding phenotypic 
diversity from developmentally stabilized (canalized) states7–10. The 
most enigmatic cohort among small-effect variants may be cryptic 
alleles1,2. In their simplest form, cryptic alleles have substantial effects 
on phenotypes only through interactions with environmental factors 
or with other alleles, including other alleles that may themselves be 
phenotypically cryptic3. Although hidden at the level of organismal 
phenotype, cryptic alleles can generate molecular phenotypes through 
altering protein function or gene expression—and are most likely to 
accumulate and remain hidden in buffered molecular contexts, such 
as redundancy within gene families and gene regulatory networks11. 
The accumulation of cryptic alleles in buffered contexts may be a 
major source of genomic variation shaping network architecture and 
trajectories of phenotypic evolution. Under this hypothesis, epistatic 
interactions between previously cryptic alleles may result in the sud-
den appearance of phenotypic variation in previously invariant traits, 
facilitating both within-species adaptation and macroevolutionary 
transitions11–13.
Demonstrating the contribution of cryptic variation to trait evolu-
tion is challenging. Genetic dissection of trait variation is typically 
confined to single species or a few closely related ones, in which only 
narrow ranges of phenotypic diversity can be assessed. Moreover, 
most dissections of natural trait variation expose only major effect 
variants, as is also true for developmental genetics in model systems, 
leaving the influence of cryptic alleles on natural populations and gene 
regulatory networks largely unexplored1,14. Importantly, background 
dependencies—probably stemming in part from cryptic alleles—are 
common in evolutionary and developmental genetics15–18. Yet, despite 
these clues, efforts to systematically dissect cryptic variation and its 
role in phenotypic evolution remain hampered by the complex and 
often poorly characterized structure and redundancy of gene regu-
latory networks, limited allelic diversity and restricted phenotypic 
resolution in most systems.
Genome editing in model systems with complex developmental pro-
grams offers a powerful approach to examine cryptic variation. Beyond 
applications in medicine and agriculture, genome editing enables 
the engineering of customized mutations and allelic series with wide
